title: "Exercises — The enzyme toolbox"
---

Pen and paper. Try each one before opening the **Hint**, and the hint before the
**Solution**: the reasoning is the point, not the answer.

Have the [NEB selection charts](https://www.neb.com/en/tools-and-resources/selection-charts)
open for every question. They list polymerase, ligase, nuclease and modifying-enzyme
properties in the same columns the lectures use. (The site blocks automated tools, so use a
browser.) Where an answer depends on the exact product, say so and name the column you would
check.

# Part 1 — Pick the enzyme and name the deciding column

## E1. Fill in without displacing

A fragment has a 5' overhang of four bases on each end and the other strand is a continuous
backbone. You want to fill in the overhang so the end is blunt, and you must **not** displace
or degrade anything. Which polymerase type, and which column decides?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Three enzymes could fill in. Two of them also do something to a strand that is in the way.
The strand in front of the filling polymerase here is the end of the duplex itself.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
**T4 DNA polymerase.** The deciding column is **strand displacement**: T4 DNA polymerase has
none, so it fills in and stops at the blunt end. Klenow also fills in, but it **displaces**,
which would cause trouble if the end were part of a nick. Taq **degrades** the downstream
strand through its 5'→3' exo, and also adds an A.

The 3'→5' exonuclease column is a bonus rather than the decider: it lets the same enzyme
trim a 3' overhang if there is one.
:::

## E2. Amplify a bisulfite-converted template

After bisulfite treatment, every unmethylated cytosine in the template has become uracil. You
want to PCR a short region. Which polymerase family can you use, and which column decides?
Name one that will fail silently.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
What does the template contain that it did not contain before the treatment? Which family
detects that base?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
The deciding column is **dU tolerance**. A Taq-type enzyme reads through uracil and works. A
high-fidelity archaeal family-B polymerase (Pfu-like, which includes the common HiFi enzymes)
has a read-ahead pocket that **stalls at uracil**, and gives little or no product. A
**uracil-tolerant** variant of the HiFi enzyme works and keeps the fidelity.

It fails "silently" in the sense that nothing is wrong with the reaction: the primers, the
buffer and the cycling are fine, and the template is not copied. If the bisulfite
control also fails, suspect the enzyme before the DNA.
:::

## E3. Copy an RNA:DNA hybrid

You have first-strand cDNA still paired with its RNA. List what the second-strand
polymerase must be able to do, and name the enzyme combination that does it.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Something has to make primers. Something has to start at them. Something has to remove the
RNA in front of the new strand.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
1. **RNase H** nicks the RNA, leaving short RNA pieces with 3'-OH ends: these are the primers
2. **RNA primer extension**: the polymerase must start from an RNA 3'-OH. Pol I does
3. **Nick extension and 5'→3' exo**: the polymerase must remove the RNA in front of it and
   keep going, which is nick translation

So the answer is **Pol I with RNase H** (the Gubler–Hoffman method). A HiFi enzyme fails the
RNA-primer column, and T4 DNA polymerase fails the nick extension one.
:::

# Part 2 — Read the row

## E4. What can this row do?

A chart row reads: **3'→5' exo: no · 5'→3' exo: no · strand displacement: strong · RT
activity: weak · 3' end: +A, partly · temperature: 60–65 °C · dU: tolerant**. For each of
these steps say *can* or *cannot*, and why:
a. end repair of sheared DNA
b. LAMP-style amplification at constant temperature
c. a proofreading library PCR
d. one-base A-tailing
e. copying a rolling-circle template

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
The row is a Bst-type large fragment. Think about which of its columns each step needs.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. **Cannot.** It displaces strands (strong) and leaves a mixed +A end, so the product is
   neither blunt nor uniform; and there is no 3'→5' exo to trim a 3' overhang.
b. **Can.** Strong displacement and 60–65 °C is the profile of isothermal amplification.
c. **Cannot.** No 3'→5' exo means no proofreading: the error rate is moderate.
d. **Partly.** It adds A, but incompletely. A dedicated A-tailing enzyme is more reliable.
e. **Can.** Strong displacement lets it roll round a circle, though phi29 is better.
:::

## E5. And this one?

A second row reads: **3'→5' exo: strong · 5'→3' exo: no · strand displacement: none · 3' end:
blunt · temperature: 12–37 °C · dU: tolerant · RT: no**. What is the enzyme type, and which
of the steps in E4 can it do?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
It is a **T4 DNA polymerase**. It can do (a) end repair, because it fills in and trims and
leaves a blunt end without displacing anything. It cannot do (b), (c), (d) or (e): it is
not thermostable, has no displacement, and leaves a blunt end rather than +A. It could be used
for **gap filling** that must not disturb the neighbouring strand.
:::

## E6. When does fidelity matter?

Library PCR runs 10 doublings on a 300 bp insert. Estimate the mean number of polymerase
errors per molecule for a Taq-class enzyme at 1e-4 per base per doubling, and for a
high-fidelity enzyme at 1e-6. Sequencing error is about 1e-3 per base. Which one dominates
the differences you see in the reads, and for which application would you still choose the
high-fidelity enzyme?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Mean errors ≈ length × rate × doublings.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
Taq-class: 300 × 1e-4 × 10 = **0.3** errors per molecule. High-fidelity: 300 × 1e-6 × 10 =
**0.003**. Sequencing: 300 × 1e-3 = **0.3** errors per read.

For counting reads, the three numbers say that the sequencer already contributes as many
errors as the Taq-class PCR, so fidelity is not the bottleneck. You would still choose the
high-fidelity enzyme for **low-frequency variants**, for **long amplicons** (more bases, more
doublings) and for **cloning**, where the error you introduce becomes a sequence you keep.
These are illustrative orders of magnitude and the real rates depend on the assay.
:::

# Part 3 — Traps and silent failures

## E7. The blocker that started priming

A PCR uses a 3'-C3-spacer "blocker" oligo to suppress amplification of a wild-type allele.
With a standard Taq polymerase it works. After switching to a proofreading polymerase for
better fidelity, the wild-type allele amplifies as well as the mutant. Why? Give two fixes.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
What does a proofreading enzyme do to an unpaired or unusual 3' end?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
The **3'→5' exonuclease** removes the spacer and the last bases of the blocker, exposing a
3'-OH that the polymerase then extends. The block was chemical, and the enzyme has an
activity that undoes chemistry at the 3' end.

Fixes: (1) use a polymerase **without** 3'→5' exo for that reaction; (2) protect the 3' end
of the blocker with **phosphorothioate bonds** so the exonuclease cannot chew in. A third
option is a blocker whose 3' end has mismatches to the template, so it cannot be extended
even after trimming.
:::

## E8. The strand information that vanished

A stranded RNA-seq library uses dUTP in the second strand and a polymerase that cannot read
uracil. After a supplier change the library still works, but about half of the reads align
to the wrong strand. The library QC is normal. What changed, and why did nothing warn you?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
The new polymerase is **uracil-tolerant**. The dU strand is no longer excluded, so both
strands amplify and the library is unstranded. Nothing warns you because both strands give
perfectly good reads; the library concentration, size and yield all look right.

The defence is a **strandedness check on a spike-in or a known gene** in every batch, and a
rule that any change to the polymerase in a dUTP-marked protocol is a change to a critical
property (the dU tolerance column).
:::

## E9. Which adapter strand needs the phosphate?

You order the two strands of a double-stranded adapter with a single 3' T overhang. Strand X
(the one carrying the 3' T) is ordered **with** a 5'-phosphate; strand Y (the other) is
ordered **without**. The inserts are end-repaired and A-tailed, so they carry 5'-phosphates.
Predict what happens at the junction on each strand. Then predict it again if the inserts
have been dephosphorylated.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Draw the junction. Which adapter 5' end meets the insert's 3'-A, and which adapter 3' end
meets the insert's 5' end? A ligase needs a 5'-P on whichever strand supplies the 5' side.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
The adapter's **3'-T** (strand X) meets the insert's **5' end**: the phosphate comes from the
insert, so this strand joins. Strand X's own 5'-phosphate is at the far end of the adapter
and is not used. Strand Y's **5' end** meets the insert's **3'-A**: here the adapter must
supply the phosphate and does not, so this strand is **not joined** and a **nick** remains.
The molecule is a usable library template, and PCR melts the nick open.

If the inserts are dephosphorylated as well, neither junction has a 5'-phosphate. Nothing
joins covalently, the single A:T pairs fall apart, and you get almost no product with no
error message. The strand that needs the phosphate is the one that supplies the 5' side of
the junction, not the one with the overhang.
:::

## E10. The two enzymes that cancel

A protocol dephosphorylates fragments with a phosphatase, adds adapters with a 5'-phosphate,
then ligates. Yield is zero. The phosphatase's inactivation step is a 10-minute incubation
at 37 °C "to save time". Explain the failure and a better design.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
A heat-labile phosphatase needs about **65 °C** to be killed. At 37 °C it is still active
when the adapters are added, and it removes the 5'-phosphate from the adapters as well as
the fragments. No end can then act as a donor.

Better: inactivate at the temperature the datasheet gives, or clean up on beads between the
two steps. A pilot that skips the phosphatase would have shown the problem at once.
:::

## E11. Pick the ligase

For each situation name a ligase type and the chart column that decides.
a. Attach a 3' adapter to a 22-nt RNA without circularising the RNA
b. Close a single-stranded DNA into a circle
c. Join an RNA to a DNA oligo, using a bridging DNA oligo
d. Join two blunt dsDNA ends at low concentration

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
For each, ask: what is the donor, and is it single or double stranded?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
a. **Truncated T4 RNA ligase 2** with a pre-adenylated, 3'-blocked adapter. Deciding column:
   *donor*: pre-adenylated, no ATP, so nothing else can join.
b. A **single-strand circularising ligase** (CircLigase-type, or T4 RNA ligase 1). Deciding
   column: *substrate* is single-stranded.
c. A **ligase for RNA:DNA hybrids** (the Chlorella virus type) on a DNA splint. Deciding
   column: *substrate*: a nick in a hybrid.
d. **T4 DNA ligase with PEG**. Blunt ends are the slowest substrate, so crowding agents and
   enzyme concentration decide. E. coli DNA ligase would not do it.
:::

## E12. The tagmentation library that would not amplify

You tagment 50 ng of human DNA with a loaded Tn5 and go straight to PCR. The DNA is
clearly fragmented on a gel, yet PCR gives almost no product. Name two causes tied to the
mechanism of tagmentation.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Hint
Two things are true of the product of the transposase immediately after the reaction. One
concerns the enzyme, the other the structure of the ends.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Solution
1. **Tn5 remains bound** to the product. It must be stripped (SDS, heat or a column) before
   PCR; otherwise the polymerase meets a protein-covered template.
2. There is a **9 nt gap** between each fragment's 3'-OH and the adapter beyond it. A
   polymerase must fill it before the primer site exists as a duplex; a protocol that
   skips the initial **72 °C extension** gives much less product.

Check also whether the loaded Tn5 was in excess (fragments too short) and whether the
adapters were loaded as two different types, since half the fragments are unproductive
by design.
:::

# Self-check

Answer without looking anything up.

1. Which polymerase property decides whether an A-tail survives?
2. Name the three things a polymerase does when it meets a strand in front of it.
3. Which column explains why a stranded-RNA-seq library loses strand information?
4. What are the two requirements for ligation to happen at a nick?
5. Why is a rSAP step heat-inactivated?
6. What does a Type IIS enzyme offer that a Type II enzyme does not?
7. What does Tn5 leave behind in the target after cutting?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="minimal"}
## Answers
1. The **3'→5' exonuclease**. If present, the A is removed; if absent, it stays.
2. It **stops**, **displaces** the strand, or **degrades** it (5'→3' exo).
3. **dU tolerance**: a polymerase that reads through uracil keeps the marked strand.
4. A **5'-phosphate** on one side and a **3'-OH** on the other, in a duplex.
5. So it does not remove the phosphate from the adapters added next.
6. It cuts **outside** its recognition site, so the overhang can be designed.
7. A **9 nt gap** beside each adapter, which a polymerase must fill.
:::

# Going further

- Open a kit manual that you use. For every enzyme named, write down its end-state in and
  out, and find the chart column that would break the step if it were wrong.
- Take the walk-through slide of the transposase deck and replace each enzyme by a wrong one:
  note which row breaks first and how you would notice.
